<!-- thm-1: body_md -->
Let $A\subset X$ be a closed subset of a compact metric space $X$, and let $d_A$ be a metric on $A$, then $d_A$ extends to $d$, a metric on $X$.
<!-- end thm-1 -->
<!-- thm-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:maintheorem}
 If $X$ is a compact metrizeable space and $R\subset X^2$ is a closed equivalence relation, and $d:R\rightarrow\mathbb{R}$ is a continuous family of metrics on the fibers, it may be extended to a metric on the entire space $X$.
<!-- end thm-2 -->
<!-- lem-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:dominatingmetric}
    Given a metric $r$ on $X/R$. There is a metric $g$ such that $g(x,y)\geq r([x],[y])$ and, in the case $x =_R y$, $g(x,y) \geq d(x,y)$.
<!-- end lem-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
Using the Tietze extension theorem for functions, extend $d$ to a continuous function $\hat{d}$ on $X^2$. We define a pseudometric $h$ such that $\hat{d}$ function will be $1$-Lipschitz with respect to $h$. $h$ is defined by
    \[ h(x,y) = \max_{z\in X} |\hat{d}(x,z) - \hat{d}(y,z)|+ \max_{z\in X}|\hat{d}(z,x)-\hat{d}(z,y)|\]
    We claim that $h$ is a pseudometric as symmetry and nonnegativity are implicit from the definition. Trivially, we have
    \[|\hat{d}(x,z) - \hat{d}(y,z)| \leq |\hat{d}(x,z) - \hat{d}(p,z)|+  |\hat{d}(p,z) - \hat{d}(y,z)|\]
      \[ |\hat{d}(z,x)-\hat{d}(z,y)| \leq  |\hat{d}(z,x)-\hat{d}(z,p)| + |\hat{d}(z,p)-\hat{d}(z,y)|\]
    for any $z$ and $p$, and so we have
    \[h(x,y)\leq h(x,p) + h(y,p)\]
    by taking maxima over $z$.\\
    $h(x,y)$ separates any points within an $R$ equivalence class, as taking $z = x$ gives $h(x,y) \geq |\hat{d}(x,x) - \hat{d}(x,y)| = d(x,y)$ for $y =_R x$. If we then define
    \[g(x,y) = h(x,y) + r([x],[y])\]
    We will get a pseudometric which separates all points in $X$, thus a metric on $X$.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- cor-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:metformet}
    $X$ is metrizeable iff $X/R$ is metrizeable, where $R$ carries a continuous family of metrics along its fibers.
<!-- end cor-1 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
This is immediate from the previous argument, without the assumption that $r$ comes from a metric on $X$.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- lem-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:metricbridge}
    Let $g(x,y)$ be a metric on a space $X$ and let $0< r < g(a,b)$, the function 
    $$f(x,y) =  \min(g(x,y), g(x,a) + r + g(b,y), g(x,b) + r + g(a,y))$$
    is a metric on $X$
<!-- end lem-2 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
Symmetry and positivity are once again clear. Furthermore this definition is invariant under interchange of $a$ and $b$.  Suppose $f(x,y) > f(x,z) + f(z,y)$ for some $z$. We must have
    \[ f(x,z) + f(z,y) <  g(x,z) + g(z,y)\]
    or else the triangle inequality for $g$ is violated.
    If we have
    \[f(x,z) \neq g(x,z) \text{ and } f(y,z) \neq g(x,z)\]
    then WLOG (by selecting $b$ to be the point closer to $z$)
    \[f(x,z) = g(x,a) + r + g(b,z) \text{ and } f(y,z) = g(y,a) + r + g(b,z)\]
    and $g(x,y) \geq f(x,y) > g(x,a) + g(a,y) $, which violates the triangle inequality. Therefore WLOG $f(x,z) = g(x,z)$ and $f(y,z) = g(y,a) + r + g(b,z) $. We must have that $g(y,a) \leq g(y,b)$, as otherwise $f(y,z) > g(y,z) $, which is impossible. Thus,
    \[f(x,y) \leq g(y,a) + r + g(b,x) \leq g(y,a) + r + g(b,z) + g(z,x) \]
    and consolidating, we obtain
    \[f(x,y) \leq f(y,z) + f(z,x)\]
    which is the triangle inequality for $f$.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
Let $A$ be the set of all metrics on $X$ for which $d_i(a,y) + d_i(x,b) \geq |d(a,b) - d(x,y) | $, dominate $r([x],[y])$ pointwise everywhere, and are dominated by $g(x,y)$ pointwise everywhere. Lemma \ref{lem:dominatingmetric} shows that this set is nonempty. Order this set by pointwise domination. Suppose we have a descending chain indexed by a linear order $(I,\leq_I)$, i.e. $d_i \leq d_j$ pointwise if $i \leq j$. Define 
   \[d_I(x,y) = \inf_{i\in I}d_i(x,y)\]
   again, symmetry and non-negativity are clear. The triangle inequality follows by splitting the infimum
   \[\inf_{i\in I}d_i(x,y) \leq \inf_{i\in I}d_i(x,z) + \inf_{i\in I}d_i(z,y)\]
   So $d_I$ is a pseudometric.
   \[d_i(a,y) + d_i(x,b) \geq |d(a,b) - d(x,y) |\]
   by assumption, and if $[x] = [y]$
   \[d_i(x,y) = d_i(x,y) + d_i(y,y) \geq |d(x,y) - d(y,y) | \geq d(x,y) \] 
   and if not then $d_i(x,y) \geq r([x],[y])$ by assumption. Taking infima yields that $d_I$ separates points and thus is a metric. Thus $d_I$ is an element of $A$. Zorn's lemma guarantees that $A$ must contain a minimal element. Call one such minimal element $\bar{d}$.\\
   Assume, in hope of a contradiction, that
   \[\bar{d}(a,b) > d(a,b)\]
   for some $a,b$ for which $d$ is defined. The function \[k(x,y) := \min(\bar{d}(x,y),\bar{d}(x,a) + d(a,b) + \bar{d}(b,y), \bar{d}(x,b) + d(b,a) + \bar{d}(a,y)  )\]
   is a metric by lemma \ref{lem:metricbridge}. Furthermore, WLOG we either have
   \[k(x,y) \geq \bar{d}(x,a) + d(a,b) + \bar{d}(b,y) \geq r([x],[a]) + r([b],[y]) \geq r([x],[y])\]
   or 
   \[k(x,y) = \bar{d}(x,y) \geq r([x],[y])\]
   so $k(x,y)$ dominates $r([x],[y])$.\\
   Furthermore
   \[ k(x,y) = \bar{d}(x,a) + d(a,b) + \bar{d}(b,y) \geq d(x,y) \]
   And so $k$ is an element of $A$, but is strictly less than $\bar{d}$, contradicting minimality. Therefore we must have that $\bar{d}(x,y) = d(x,y)$ for all $(x,y)\in R$.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
